summary: Holds, with stated conditions: earliest due date minimises the maximum lateness on the device for reads and writes together (to within one page group, about 1.5 s); the ratio greedy solves the divisible room problem; the relaxed problem's room price is the index of the marginal holder with complementary slackness; weak duality holds in the open model; the saturation identity holds; and born-clean or delay alone bounds the dirty set once writes are guaranteed more than the new-token rate (4.1 K tokens/s). Fails as drafted: (1) in an open queue mu is 1 + (Q + lam x)/(1 - rho), not 1 + Q (91 against 9 at 90 % load). (2) In the saturated loop mu is N for response time but N - B for TTFT (108, not 128); the measured 0.73 N is that minus a transient of the pausing users, and the recorded tables of campaigns 32 and 34 close to within 1 s. (3) c = P(no other ready turn) is false for the single work queue section 1.5 describes: there a stall-second costs 1.0 to 1.6 s up to about 94 % utilisation. It is about right for the engine's pool-bound batch, where an empty slot costs about the turn's own second. (4) The Lagrangian bound is not a bound in the closed loop: in a three-user example 0.2 s more GPU work lowers summed response time by 8.4 s. (5) The device fallback is optimal only when every transfer is already late; as written it costs 2.3 times the optimum on mixed instances. (6) Result 10 is not covered by the cited theorems for the joint design. Must change: state the model as a pool-bound batch in a closed loop, with mu = N - B and c = P(the slot stays empty). For the saturated regime use the floor mean TTFT >= (N - B) g0 - Z + own prefill, attained exactly when nothing is recomputed and no slot is left empty; campaign 34's arms sit about 1.6 s above it. Keep the Lagrangian as the decision rule and as a bound for the open, light-load model only, read lambda off the lowest index still held, and on the device use earliest due date while feasible and the index w / max(p, d - t) otherwise. results.name: 1. The weight mu in an open queue (section 1.5, first half; section 6)
results.statement: Model: one GPU server that serves one turn at a time, first come first served, without preemption; arrival times a_1 < a_2 < ... are fixed (open queue); turn j needs s_j seconds of GPU work; W_j is its queue wait. Add delta >= 0 seconds of work to turn k. (i) Each W_j is a convex, non-decreasing, piecewise-linear function of delta with slopes 0 or 1. (ii) The derivative of sum_j W_j at delta = 0+ is B_k, the number of turns served after k in k's busy period (the maximal stretch in which the server never idles). If the extra work comes before k's own first token, summed TTFT rises at rate mu_k = 1 + B_k. (iii) For a finite injection the rise is at least delta * B_k. (iv) If arrivals are Poisson with rate lam, work is i.i.d. with mean s_bar and rho = lam * s_bar < 1, then given Q turns waiting behind the turn in service and x seconds of its service left when the work is added, E[B_k | Q, x] = (Q + lam * x) / (1 - rho). Averaged over the turns of an M/M/1 queue E[B_k] = rho / (1 - rho)^2, while the mean queue length at a service start is rho^2 / (1 - rho).
results.proof: Step 1 (Lindley). W_{j+1} = max(0, W_j + s_j - (a_{j+1} - a_j)). Unrolling gives W_j = max over i <= j of [sum_{l=i}^{j-1} s_l - (a_j - a_i)], the term i = j being 0. Step 2. With s_k replaced by s_k + delta, term i has slope 1 in delta if i <= k < j and slope 0 otherwise. A maximum of affine functions is convex and piecewise linear; here it is non-decreasing with slopes 0 or 1. That is (i). Step 3. The right-derivative of a maximum of affine functions is the largest slope among the terms that attain the maximum. For j > k a term with i <= k attains it exactly when the server has not idled between the start of k and the arrival of j, that is when j is in k's busy period. So W_j has right-derivative 1 for those j and 0 for the others; the sum is B_k. Turn k's own first token adds 1. That is (ii). Step 4. By convexity W_j(delta) - W_j(0) >= delta * (right-derivative at 0); summing over j gives (iii). Step 5 (M/G/1). The turns served after k in its busy period are the Q waiting ones, the arrivals during the x seconds left (Poisson with mean lam * x), the arrivals during the service of each of those, and so on. Each first-generation turn heads a sub-busy period of mean size 1 + rho + rho^2 + ... = 1/(1 - rho), because a turn has on average rho arrivals during its own service. Hence E[B_k | Q, x] = (Q + lam x)/(1 - rho). For M/M/1 at a service start E[Q] = rho^2/(1 - rho) and x = s with mean s_bar, so E[B_k] = (rho^2/(1 - rho) + rho)/(1 - rho) = rho/(1 - rho)^2. QED.
results.draft_claim_checked: Section 1.5: 'In an open queue mu is about 1 + Q (queue length)'. Section 6: 'mu(t), GPU time: 1 + the number of ready turns waiting'. Both understate. The turns delayed are all later turns of the busy period, including those that have not arrived yet: mu = 1 + (Q + lam x)/(1 - rho) in expectation, the queue length divided by the slack 1 - rho. At rho = 0.9 the mean is 91 against 1 + Q = 9. 1 + Q is a lower bound, exact only when no turn arrives before the queue drains.

results.name: 2. The weight mu in the closed loop: N for response time, N - B for TTFT (section 1.5)
results.statement: Model: N users stay in session; each alternates a pause (given by the trace) and one request; a request is in the system from its arrival to its last token. Over a window of length T let X = requests completed / T, R = mean time in the system, Z = (time-average number of pausing users) / X. (a) Accounting, with no assumption on the server: N / X = R + Z. (b) Single server (one request at a time, never idle on the window). Add delta seconds to the work of the request in service at time t0, delta small enough that the order of service does not change. Then exactly one request of every user is delayed by delta and no other response time changes: the sum of response times rises by N * delta. If every request gets eps more work, mean R rises by N * eps. (c) Below saturation, in steady state, mu := d(mean R)/d(work per request) = N * (1 - a), where a in [0, 1] is the share of an added GPU-second that displaces idle time. (d) Pool-bound batch (the engine): at most B turns run; prefill is serial and pauses decoding; a decode step with n running turns takes tau(n) seconds and gives each of them one token. If the pool is always full and never short of ready turns, then GPU time per request is g = 1/X = P + tau(B) * n_out / B (P = mean prefill seconds per request including recompute, n_out = mean output tokens), the mean time between admission and last token is B / X, and mean TTFT = (N - B)/X - Z + t_pre (t_pre = mean time from admission to first token). One more second of prefill work at time t0 raises the sum of response times by N and the sum of TTFT by N - B_dec, where B_dec is the number of running turns already past their first token.
results.proof: (a) At every instant each of the N users is either pausing or has a request in the system, so N * T = integral of (number pausing) + integral of (number in the system). The second integral is the summed time in system of the requests of the window, up to the requests cut by its two ends. Divide by X * T. (b) The server is never idle, so the m-th service completion after t0 happens at (completion of the request in service at t0) + (sum of the next m works). The order is unchanged, so every completion after t0 moves by exactly delta, and so does every later service start (a start is the previous completion). Take a user u. If u has a request in the system at t0, that request completes delta later and its arrival does not move: +delta. If u is pausing at t0, its next arrival does not move (the pause began before t0) and its start moves by delta: +delta. After that delayed request u's next arrival = completion + pause moves by delta, and so do its start and completion: no change, and the same for all its later requests. So each user loses delta once: N * delta. The order is unchanged whenever delta is smaller than the smallest distance between a moved arrival and an unmoved one, which is positive with probability one for continuous pause laws. The sustained statement is (a) with X = 1/g: R = N * g - Z. (c) In general 1/X = g + i with i the GPU idle time per request, so dR/dg = N * (1 + di/dg) = N * (1 - a), a = -di/dg. (d) In T seconds the GPU spends X*T*P on prefill and the rest on decode steps; (T - X*T*P)/tau(B) steps give B tokens each and must supply X*T*n_out tokens, so X * (P + tau(B) n_out / B) = 1. Little's law on the running set (always B turns) gives B/X between admission and completion; on the queue it gives (N - B)/X - Z of queue wait; TTFT = queue wait + t_pre. Single injection: all GPU events after t0 move by delta (the GPU is never idle and admissions happen at completions). The B_dec turns past their first token finish delta later: response +delta, TTFT unchanged. Every other user (being prefilled, admitted, queued or pausing) gets its next first token delta later, and after its delayed request its whole timeline is shifted, as in (b). Total: N for response, N - B_dec for TTFT. QED.

results.name: 3. The lateness weight c under pass-over (sections 1.5, 5.3, 6)
results.statement: Model A (one server, the work queue of section 1.5): turn i arrives at a_i and is ready (its read has landed) at l_i >= a_i; whenever the server is free it starts the earliest-arrived ready turn. D_i = the time i would start if it were ready; stall S = l_i - D_i > 0; s_j = GPU work of turn j. (L1) If the server is never idle from D_i until i starts, and J = (j_1..j_m) are the turns started in between (the jumpers), the summed wait of all turns changes by exactly sum_{j in J} s_j - m * s_i. That is 0 for equal work, 0 in expectation when the jumpers' work is i.i.d. with the same mean as s_i, and about (1 - s_i / s_bar) per second of stall otherwise (s_bar = mean work of the jumpers). (L2) If no other turn is ready during the stall, the summed wait rises by S * (1 + B_i) for small S, B_i = later turns in i's busy period: an idle GPU-second is priced like a second of work (result 1). (L3) In a stable open M/M/1 queue with exchangeable work the expected cost per second of stall is 1 + rho for short stalls and tends to 1 for long ones. (L4) Closed loop: late reads change the mean TTFT only through throughput; with the same work per request, change of mean TTFT = N * (change of GPU idle time per request); it is 0 when the GPU never idles, whatever the differences in work between turns (over a finite window a policy that delays heavier turns completes more requests, a composition effect). Model B (pool-bound batch of result 2(d)): (L5) a stalled turn costs its own second while the slot it would take stays empty, and nothing in the mean while another ready turn takes it. An empty slot also loses a / (B * tau(B)) GPU-seconds per second (a = fixed part of the decode step), worth N * a / (B tau(B)) seconds of summed response time in the saturated loop: 0.96 at N = 128, B = 20, a = 3.5 ms, tau = 23.3 ms.
results.proof: (L1) Without the stall the order from D_i on is i, j_1, .., j_m, rest; with it the order is j_1, .., j_m, i, rest, with no idle time. Turn i starts sum_J s_j later. Each jumper starts s_i earlier (a jumper that arrives during the stall finds the server busy in both schedules). After i's service both schedules have done the same work without idling, so every later start is the same. Sum: sum_J s_j - m s_i. m is the first index at which the jumpers' cumulative work reaches S, a stopping time, so by Wald E[sum_J s_j] = E[m] * s_bar, and E[m * s_i] = E[m] E[s_i] when s_i is independent of the jumpers: the expectation is E[m] (s_bar - E s_i). (L2) i starts S later; this is result 1 with S more seconds of work on i before its start. (L3) Short stall: with probability P0 = P(no turn waits behind i at D_i) the server idles for S, and each idle second delays i and the later turns of its busy period, 1 + rho/(1 - rho) = 1/(1 - rho) turns in expectation (result 1 with Q = 0). Otherwise a waiting turn j is started, i waits for all of s_j and j gains s_i: zero in expectation. The turns behind i at D_i are the arrivals during its wait; in M/M/1 the wait is 0 with probability 1 - rho and exponential with rate (1 - rho)/s_bar otherwise, so P0 = (1 - rho) + rho (1 - rho) = 1 - rho^2 and the cost is (1 - rho^2)/(1 - rho) = 1 + rho per second. Long stall: i loses S plus a bounded residual wait; for the others, i's work is removed at D_i and inserted again S later into a queue that has forgotten the removal; each insertion delays a number of turns whose mean is finite and does not depend on S, so the others' change is bounded and the cost is S + O(1). (L4) Result 2(a): mean R = N/X - Z and 1/X = work per request + idle per request. (L5) The turn's own delay is immediate. A fixed set of requests needs sum n_out tokens = (number of steps) * B when the pool is full; k steps with one slot empty waste k slot-steps, that is k/B extra steps, each costing the fixed part a (the per-turn part of a step is spent only when the turn decodes). One slot-second empty is 1/tau(B) steps, so the loss is a/(B tau(B)) GPU-seconds, priced at N by result 2. QED.
results.draft_claim_checked: Sections 1.5 (c), 5.3 and 6: 'a second of stall costs c(t) = P(no other ready turn when turn i is due): about 1 at light load, about 0 once ready work always waits', estimated as 'the share of recent admissions made with no other ready turn waiting'. The two ends are right. In between it is false for the work queue that 1.5 describes: the cost is P(the GPU idles during the stall) times the price of an idle GPU-second, and the product stays at or above 1 at every stable open load and up to about 94 % utilisation in the closed loop (measured 1.0 to 1.1 where the draft's two estimators give 0.07 to 0.6). 'That turn is admitted earlier by about the same amount' needs (1) ready work behind the stalled turn for the whole stall, not one ready turn when it is due, and (2) in the open model, jumpers with the same mean work as the stalled turn. Counterexamples: a stalled 0.1 s turn in front of 1 s turns costs 0.9 per stall-second although ready work always waits; a stalled 5 s turn gains 4 per stall-second; a lone stalled turn costs 1 + B_i, up to 36 in the test. For the engine's pool-bound batch the draft's c is about right (within 0.1 in simulation), because an empty slot costs about the turn's own second; there the precise form is c * S = E[(stall - time for which ready turns keep the slot filled)+]. It is a statement about the mean: the stalled turn itself always loses its stall.

results.name: 4. Order on the device: Jackson, Horn, and what happens when due dates cannot be met (sections 3.4, 5.2; result 4)
results.statement: The device is one machine of beta tokens per second. A transfer j (read or write) has a release time r_j, a size p_j (device-seconds) and a due date d_j (a read: its turn's admission time T_j; a write: the time d_w at which its host copy would be given up). C_j = completion, lateness C_j - d_j, tardiness (C_j - d_j)+. (a) Jackson 1955: all jobs available, no preemption: serving in non-decreasing due date minimises the maximum lateness. (b) Horn 1974: with release times and preemption at any instant, always serving the released unfinished job with the earliest due date minimises the maximum lateness; the optimum is L* = max over pairs (r, d) of [r + work of the jobs released at or after r and due by d - d]. Corollary (feasibility): if any schedule meets every due date, this one does. (c) If a transfer can be interrupted only between pieces of at most p_max device-seconds, earliest due date over released pieces has maximum lateness below L* + p_max, and it is not always optimal. (d) (a) to (c) hold for reads alone and for reads and writes together: they use only release times, sizes and due dates, and dividing the device's rate between a read stream and a write stream cannot beat serving one job at a time. With free room a write has no due date and goes after every due read. (e) These are statements about the maximum lateness in seconds. The design's objective on the device is the weighted tardiness sum_j w_j (C_j - d_j)+, w_j = c_j for a read and lambda * L_p for a write. Earliest due date minimises it exactly when it meets every due date (value 0). When every waiting job is already late the objective is sum w_j C_j minus a constant and Smith's ratio rule (largest w_j / p_j first) is optimal. In between the problem is NP-hard (strongly so with weights) and neither rule, nor the two combined, is optimal. Stochastic counterparts: with linear waiting costs the c-mu rule (priority to the largest cost rate over mean size) minimises the long-run average cost of a multi-class M/G/1 queue among non-idling, non-anticipating policies (Cox and Smith 1961); with convex increasing delay costs C_k the generalised c-mu rule (serve the class with the largest C_k'(age of its oldest job) over mean size) is optimal in the heavy-traffic limit (van Mieghem 1995). For the tardiness cost the derivative is 0 before the due date and w_k after it, so that rule says 'among late transfers, largest w/p' and is silent among the others; the kink is outside the theorem's smoothness assumptions, so this is guidance, not a proof. (f) With a precedence 'this write must finish before that read can start' (the read needs the room the write cleans), earliest due date on the modified dates d'_w = min(d_w, T_j - p_j) minimises the maximum lateness among the orders that respect the precedence (Lawler 1973). (g) In the saturated loop a late read costs nothing in the mean while ready turns wait (result 3), so every order that keeps the GPU supplied ties on the mean, and earliest due date is then optimal for the second criterion, the longest stall of a reader.
results.proof: (a) Take an optimal order with adjacent jobs i before j and d_i > d_j, starting at t. After swapping, j completes earlier, and i completes at t + p_i + p_j, the old completion of j, with lateness t + p_i + p_j - d_i < t + p_i + p_j - d_j, the old lateness of j. The maximum does not rise; repeat until sorted. (b) Lower bound: the jobs released at or after r and due by d cannot start before r, so the last of them completes at or after r + their work. Attainment: let j* have the largest lateness under the rule, completing at C, and let t1 be the start of the last stretch ending at C in which only jobs due by d_{j*} are served without idling. Just before t1 the machine idles or serves a job due later than d_{j*}; in both cases no job served in [t1, C] was released before t1, or the rule would have served it. So these jobs are released at or after t1, due by d_{j*}, and need at least C - t1 of work: the bound gives L* >= C - d_{j*}. (c) Same argument: the later-due piece that runs just before t1 started at t0 > t1 - p_max, when none of the jobs served in [t1, C] was released, so in any schedule their last completion is after t0 + (C - t1) > C - p_max. (d) Any division of the device's rate is a limit of preemptive one-at-a-time schedules with the same completion times, so (b) covers it; the engine's device delivered about 2.1 GB/s whatever the read/write split. (e) Maximum lateness at most 0 means all tardiness is 0. If every d_j is in the past, (C_j - d_j)+ = C_j - d_j; for adjacent i before j starting at t the cost w_i (t + p_i) + w_j (t + p_i + p_j) is at most the swapped cost iff w_i / p_i >= w_j / p_j (Smith 1956). Hardness: Lawler 1977 and Lenstra, Rinnooy Kan and Brucker 1977 (weighted), Du and Leung 1990 (unweighted). Counterexamples in between, weights 1 unless given: jobs (work, due) = (10, 9), (1, 9.5): earliest due date costs 2.5, the other order 2.0. Jobs (work, due, weight) = (10, 10, 1), (1, 100, 5), (5, 12, 1): Smith's order costs 6, the optimum 3. (f) The modified dates are no later than the originals, so the maximum lateness can only grow. Conversely, if the write's modified lateness exceeds its original one, then d'_w = T_j - p_j, and the read starts after the write, so C_j - T_j >= C_w + p_j - T_j = C_w - d'_w: the read is at least as late. So on precedence-feasible orders the two maxima are equal. Sorting by d' puts the write before its read (d'_w < T_j) and by (a) minimises the maximum for the modified dates. (g) Result 3 (L1, L4) and (b). QED.

results.name: 5. Preempt on host room: the covering knapsack and the greedy bound (section 5.1; result 5)
results.statement: A read needs m tokens of host room. Holder j has L_j tokens and displacing it costs C_j >= 0 (the rise of its priced cost at the current prices). Problem: minimise sum_j C_j x_j subject to sum_j L_j x_j >= m, x_j in {0, 1}. (a) Divisible version (0 <= x_j <= 1, cost proportional to the part taken): taking holders in increasing C_j / L_j, the last one (the critical holder k) in part, is optimal; its value Z_LP is a lower bound on the 0-1 optimum OPT. (b) 0-1 version: taking whole holders in that order until m is covered costs less than Z_LP + C_k, hence less than OPT plus the cost of one holder, and frees less than L_k tokens beyond m. (c) The ratio to OPT is unbounded. (d) A variant with ratio at most 2: walk the same order; a holder that would complete the cover is recorded as a candidate (the holders taken so far plus this one) and skipped; return the cheapest candidate. Assumptions behind the knapsack itself: costs add up across holders (fixed prices: displacing several holders does not move kappa or lambda) and, for (a), the cost of a partial eviction is proportional to the tokens taken.
results.proof: (a) Exchange: if a solution takes part of a holder with a larger ratio while a holder with a smaller ratio is not fully taken, moving a token of room from the first to the second keeps the room and does not raise the cost; repeating reaches the greedy solution. (b) Greedy takes holders 1..k whole: cost = Z_LP + (1 - x_k) C_k < Z_LP + C_k <= OPT + C_k; the surplus is (1 - x_k) L_k < L_k. (c) m = 1; holder A has 1 token and cost 1; holder B has M tokens and cost 0.9 M. B has the smaller ratio and is taken first: cost 0.9 M against 1. (d) Call a holder big if the walk skipped it and small if it took it. The small holders never cover m, so an optimal set contains a big holder; let k be the first big holder in the order with C_k <= OPT, and S the small holders before it. Big holders before k cost more than OPT, so they are not in the optimal set, which therefore uses, among the holders before k, only members of S. The optimal set covers m and S does not, so the tokens of the optimal set outside S exceed the tokens of S outside the optimal set, and they have ratios at least as large; hence cost(optimal set outside S) >= cost(S outside optimal set), so cost(S) <= OPT. The candidate S plus k costs at most 2 OPT. QED.

(2) The order written in 5.1 (ended sessions; clean idle prefixes by nu; staged reads; queued turns) is a fixed order of classes, not a ratio order; it is the knapsack order only if the classes' cost-per-token ranges do not overlap. The entries also mix units: nu is a cost per token-second, the staged-read score is a cost per token, and the queued-turn score is not divided by L_j. One list by C_j / L_j is needed, with C_j / L_j = sup over horizons h of [(K_j / L_j) F_j(h | a) - lambda * tau_j(h | a)], the surplus per token of keeping j at the current price (positive exactly when nu_j > lambda). results.name: 6. Price: the relaxed problem, the marginal holder, complementary slackness, and the frontier estimate (section 6; result 6)
results.statement: Relaxed joint problem (open model). Session i controls the host tokens it holds m_i(t), its use of the device u_i(t) in {0, 1} and its SSD tokens s_i(t). Its cost is Phi_i = E sum over its requests of [c S + mu gamma U] (S = stall seconds, U = recomputed tokens, gamma = GPU seconds per token), with the weights c and mu, the arrivals and the queue waits given. Hard constraints at every t: sum_i m_i <= C_H, sum_i u_i <= 1, sum_i s_i <= C_S. Relaxed constraints: the same on average over [0, T]. Lagrangian with lambda, kappa, sigma >= 0: sum_i Phi_i + lambda (E int sum_i m_i - C_H T) + kappa (E int sum_i u_i - T) + sigma (E int sum_i s_i - C_S T) = sum_i J_i - (lambda C_H + kappa + sigma C_S) T, with J_i as in section 1.6. Theorem (room price). Assume that for every price lambda >= 0 an optimal policy of session i for J_i holds its prefix in state x exactly when its index nu_i(x) >= lambda, and that 'nu > lambda' is optimal too (the holding problem is indexable with index nu). Let M+(lambda) and M-(lambda) be the total expected host tokens demanded under 'hold iff nu > lambda' and 'hold iff nu >= lambda', and lambda* = inf{lambda >= 0 : M+(lambda) <= C_H}. (i) If M+(0) <= C_H then lambda* = 0 and the unpriced policies are optimal for the relaxed problem. (ii) Otherwise M+(lambda*) <= C_H <= M-(lambda*), and the policy that holds when nu > lambda*, drops when nu < lambda*, and holds with a probability theta when nu = lambda* (theta chosen so that demand equals C_H) is optimal for the relaxed problem, with multiplier lambda*. So lambda* is the index of the holders at the margin and lambda* (demand - C_H) = 0. (iii) Online estimate. Evicting the lowest index, and only when room is needed, fills the room in decreasing index; that is the primal optimum of the instant problem 'maximise sum_j nu_j L_j x_j subject to sum_j L_j x_j <= C_H, 0 <= x_j <= 1', and its dual variable is the index at which the room runs out: lambda(t) = the lowest index still held, 0 while room is free. Primal and dual come from the same sort, with no step size and no iteration. Dual ascent (lambda <- lambda * exp(eta (d - C)/C)) instead iterates on the price with excess demand as its gradient; a hard capacity censors the excess at 0 unless refusals and forced evictions are counted, and it takes many intervals to converge. (iv) sigma: the same theorem with SSD tokens, C_S and the index of a stored chain (tail before head, because a lookup stops at the first missing page). (v) kappa and mu are prices of a different kind: kappa(t) = the summed lateness cost rate of the transfers that complete late after t in the device's busy period; it is what one more unit of device capacity at t would save.
results.proof: Decoupling: for fixed multipliers each term of the Lagrangian depends on one session's own controls (weights and arrivals are given), so it is minimised session by session. Sufficiency (Everett 1963): let pi* be the policy of (ii). Both rules minimise J_i at price lambda*, and so does a mixture decided by a coin flipped at each return, whose demand moves linearly from M+(lambda*) to M-(lambda*). M+ is non-increasing and right-continuous and M- is its left limit, so M+(lambda*) <= C_H <= M-(lambda*) and a theta with demand exactly C_H exists. For any policy pi that meets the relaxed constraint: cost(pi) >= cost(pi) + lambda* (demand(pi) - C_H) >= cost(pi*) + lambda* (demand(pi*) - C_H) = cost(pi*). The first step uses demand(pi) <= C_H, the second that pi* minimises the Lagrangian, the third demand(pi*) = C_H (or lambda* = 0 in case (i)). Holders with nu above lambda* are kept and those below dropped, so lambda* is the index at the margin. Instant problem: its dual is 'minimise lambda C_H + sum_j L_j (nu_j - lambda)+ over lambda >= 0', whose optimum is the index of the critical holder in the fill by decreasing index (0 if everything fits). The two agree in a stationary system with many holders: the frontier is the empirical quantile of the holders' indices at which cumulative tokens reach C_H, and lambda* is the same quantile of the expected distribution. Device price: one more unit of work at t in front of the transfers behind moves the completion of each later transfer of the busy period by one unit, so sum_j w_j (C_j - d_j)+ rises by the weights of those that complete late; one more unit of capacity is the mirror image. QED.
results.draft_claim_checked: Section 6 and result 6: 'lambda(t): the index nu of the marginal holder (the highest index among the pages given up lately); 0 while room is free. This is the multiplier of the room constraint in the relaxed problem ... read off the eviction frontier, not learned from refusals'; 'sigma(t): the index of the cleaner's marginal victim'; 'kappa(t): the summed lateness cost rate of the transfers waiting behind'. What holds: the theorem, given indexability of the holding problem (result 2, not checked here beyond the toy) and a relaxation on average; lambda* is a constant, lambda(t) is the multiplier of the instant problem. What differs. (1) 'The highest index among the pages given up lately' is biased upward with the length of 'lately' (2 % at 5 s, 7 % at 30 s, 19 % at 600 s in the toy); the time-average of the lowest index still held is unbiased (1.00 lambda*). (2) lambda sits inside the index through K_read (the term lambda L r), so the frontier solves lambda = (a + lambda r) h, that is lambda = a h / (1 - r h); harmless while r h is small. (3) The frontier prices a marginal token; a 25 K-token read is 1.5 to 3 % of the room and its cost is the knapsack cost of result 5, not lambda times m. (4) A price that is too low is harmless while eviction is by index and only on need (cost +0.5 % at 0.1 lambda*); a price that is too high wastes room (+38 % at 2 lambda*): never drop a holder for the price while room is free. (5) kappa as drafted counts only the transfers waiting now and already late; the exact price also counts transfers that arrive later in the busy period and those that become late. In the test the draft's estimator is 3 to 14 % of the exact value. (6) Room prices (lambda, sigma) are indices of marginal holders; server prices (mu, kappa) are cost rates of the work behind in the busy period. Section 0's 'the length of each queue is a price' holds for neither kind without the factor 1/(1 - load).

results.name: 7. The bound: weak duality in the open model, and why it fails in the closed loop (sections 1.6, 7; result 7)
results.statement: For every lambda, kappa, sigma >= 0 let D = sum_i J_i* - (lambda C_H + kappa + sigma C_S) T, where J_i* is the smallest value of J_i over the policies of session i alone (alone, a session has no line at the device and no limit on room, and pays the prices). Then for every policy pi that meets the three hard constraints with the same information, the cost sum_i E[c S_i + mu gamma U_i] under pi is at least D. Assumptions: (A1) open model: arrivals, queue waits and the weights c and mu do not depend on the policy; (A2) sessions' gaps are independent of each other given the hints (or J_i* is taken over policies that may use everything the joint policy knows); (A3) every held token is charged to one session (no shared pages, or shared pages charged in parts adding up to at most one); (A4) J_i* is computed with the line wait V = 0. In the open first-come-first-served queue without pass-over, taking mu_k = 1 + B_k on the path with no recompute makes base + sum_k mu_k gamma U_k a true lower bound on summed TTFT, so D extends to summed TTFT there. In the closed loop the statement is false as a bound on summed TTFT.
results.proof: Step 1. A policy that meets the hard constraints at every instant meets them on average, so each penalty term is at most 0 and sum_i Phi_i(pi) >= Lagrangian(pi). Step 2. Lagrangian(pi) = sum_i J_i(pi) - (lambda C_H + kappa + sigma C_S) T, where J_i(pi) uses the holdings, device use and SSD use that pi gives session i. Step 3. Seen from session i the other sessions' states are outside randomness; by A1 and A2 they carry no information about i's future beyond its own hint, and by A4 any schedule that pi gives i, waiting in line included, is also available to i alone. So J_i(pi) >= J_i*. Step 4. Combine: sum_i Phi_i(pi) >= D. Open first-come-first-served extension: by result 1 the sum of waits is convex in the vector of works, so it is at least its linearisation at the no-recompute path, whose slopes are the B_k of that path and do not depend on the policy. Closed loop, counterexample: three users and one first-come-first-served server. A needs 5 s and then, 0.9 s after its reply, 10 s; B needs 1 s twice (arriving at 0.1 s, then 0.001 s after its reply); C sends one 1 s request at 5.95 s. The five requests have a summed response time of 44.05 s. With 0.2 s more work on A's first request it is 35.65 s: A returns 0.2 s later and C's short request now goes before A's long one. More work, lower cost; so no bound of the form base + mu * work holds there, and D added to the base is not a lower bound. QED.

Holds with four additions. (1) It bounds the unpriced cost sum E[c S + mu gamma U], not a 'priced cost'. (2) The per-session problems must be solved without the device's line: section 2 puts the measured line wait V inside r, which is right for the decision rule and wrong for the bound. (3) Shared prefix heads must not be charged in full to every sharer (17 % of prompt tokens are held by earlier sessions). (4) 'The same hints' is essential: a policy that knows each gap exactly is 13 to 25 % below the bound in the toy. With constant prices the device term is nearly empty: the average device constraint is slack unless the device is busy all the time, so the bound ignores the read line, which is most of r in the records. In the closed loop of the replay, which is section 1.5's own setting for mu = N, it bounds nothing; the usable statement there is the floor of result 8.

results.name: 8. Saturation: the identity, the tie between policies, and a tight floor (result 8; section 8)
results.statement: Setting: N users in session throughout a window; pauses given by the trace; the pool-bound batch GPU of result 2(d). (a) For any policy, mean TTFT = N/X - Z - D_run + t_pre exactly, with X the completion rate, Z = (time-average number of pausing users)/X, D_run = (time-average number of running turns)/X, t_pre the mean time from admission to first token. (b) If under two policies the pool is always full while turns wait (B running), the prefill seconds per request P are the same (new tokens, recompute and per-batch overhead), and the same requests complete (same mean pause and output length), then X and the mean TTFT are the same, whatever the timing of reads, the order on the device and the turns that wait. (c) Floor: for every policy under which the system stays saturated, mean TTFT >= (N - B) g0 - Z + p0, where g0 = P0 + tau(B) n_out / B is the GPU time per request with no recompute and a full pool and p0 is the mean prefill time of a request's own new tokens. A policy reaches the floor (up to prefill queueing after admission) when nothing is recomputed and no slot is left empty while a turn waits; its distance from the floor is (N - B) times its wasted GPU seconds per request, recompute plus the loss from empty slots. (d) What matters where, with FA3 constants: the pool fills at about N_sat = B + Z / g0 = 20 + 22/0.46 = 68 users in session. Below about 50 users every second of exposed stall costs about one second and a GPU-second costs 1 to a few: Fetch timing and Retain order act directly. Above about 72 users only wasted GPU seconds move the mean: Retain, Preempt and the write path matter through recompute (never lose the only copy, never refuse a read), and Fetch and the device order matter only for keeping some ready turn available and for who waits. Between the two both act.
results.proof: (a) Result 2(a), with the system split into queue and running set, and TTFT = queue wait + t_pre. (b) By result 2(d) 1/X = P + tau(B) n_out / B depends only on P, B and n_out; insert in (a) with D_run = B/X. (c) Recompute adds gamma U to P. An empty slot lowers the tokens per step from B to B - 1 at step time tau(B - 1), and (B - 1)/tau(B - 1) < B/tau(B) because tau has a positive fixed part. Both raise 1/X above g0. With fewer than B running, N - (number running) is larger as well, so (N - running)/X >= (N - B) g0. t_pre is at least the turn's own prefill, mean p0. Insert in (a). (d) The pool is full when the pausing users, X * Z at most Z/g0, plus B fall short of N; the regimes then follow from results 2 and 3. QED.

results.name: 9. Stability: the smallest model of campaign 32's loop and the two rules that remove it (result 9)
results.statement: Model: d(t) = dirty tokens in host memory (pages whose SSD write is pending; they cannot be evicted). p(d) = share of reads refused for lack of clean room, non-decreasing in d, 0 for d <= d0, at most p_max. A refused read is recomputed: GPU time per request g(p) = g0 + gamma L p (L = history tokens, gamma = seconds per token), request rate x(p) = 1/g(p) in the saturated loop. Each request writes Dw new tokens; without the born-clean rule the recomputed L p tokens are written again. Writes drain at w tokens per second while d > 0. So d' = F(d) - w, F(d) = x(p(d)) (Dw + L p(d)). (a) Without the two rules F increases with p whenever g0 > gamma Dw (0.46 s against 0.08 s here). With a_max := Dw / g0 and a_loop := (Dw + L p_max)/(g0 + gamma L p_max): if w < a_max the dirty set grows from 0; if a_max < w < a_loop the state d = 0 is stable, there is an unstable point d_u with p(d_u) = p* = (w g0 - Dw)/(L (1 - w gamma)), and above d_u the dirty set runs away to the room's limit (two stable states); if w > a_loop only d = 0 remains. Near d_u the excess grows like exp(t / T_e), 1/T_e = p'(d_u) L (g0 - gamma Dw) x(p*)^2. (b) Born clean (a recomputed page that the SSD holds complete is not written again): F(d) = Dw x(p(d)) <= a_max for every d. If the writes are guaranteed w_min > a_max, then d(t) <= sup_s [A(s, t) - w_min (t - s)], at most the burst allowance of the new-token process A, for all t and whatever the refusals. (c) Delay instead of refusal (a read that finds no room waits): p = 0, nothing is recomputed for lack of room, the same bound holds and the request rate stays 1/g0; it needs waiting reads not to hold room that only their own progress would free. So each rule alone removes the runaway in this model; born-clean leaves the recompute of refused reads, delay removes it.
results.proof: (a) dF/dp = L (g0 - gamma Dw)/(g0 + gamma L p)^2 > 0, and p is non-decreasing in d, so F is non-decreasing in d with F(0) = a_max. d' = F(d) - w changes sign from negative to positive where F(d_u) = w, that is Dw + L p = w (g0 + gamma L p), p* = (w g0 - Dw)/(L (1 - w gamma)). Such a point exists in the range of p exactly when a_max < w < a_loop. It is unstable because F is increasing there; d = 0 is stable because F(0) < w. Linearising d' at d_u gives the rate. (b) With born-clean every token enters the dirty set at most once, when first produced. Requests complete at rate at most 1/g0, since recompute only slows them, so new tokens arrive at rate at most a_max plus bursts. A work-conserving server of rate at least w_min > a_max has backlog sup_s [A(s, t) - w_min (t - s)], which the burst allowance bounds. (c) The same with p = 0. QED.

results.name: 10. Many sessions: what index-policy theory gives and what it does not (result 10)
results.statement: What the cited theory gives (from memory; to be checked against the papers). Weber and Weiss (1990): N identical restless bandits with finitely many states, a fixed share of them active at a time; if the bandits are indexable and the differential equation of the index policy's fluid limit has a single globally attracting fixed point, the index policy's reward per bandit converges to the value of the relaxed problem as N grows. They give counterexamples with four states in which the fluid limit cycles and the index policy is not asymptotically optimal. Verloop (2016): the same for several classes of bandits that may arrive and depart, for a set of priority policies built from the relaxed linear programme (Whittle's index policy among them when indexable), again under a global-attractor condition. Brown and Smith (2020): finite horizon, non-identical and non-stationary items; the gap between a Lagrangian index policy with careful tie-breaking and the Lagrangian bound is of order sqrt(N) while the value is of order N; no indexability or attractor condition, but one resource, two actions per item and independent items. What these support here: in the open model restricted to Retain (hold or drop, restore cost K given, sessions independent given their hints, finitely many hint classes, room C_H growing in proportion to N, each prefix small against the room), 'evict the lowest index when room is needed' has a cost per session that converges to the relaxed bound of result 7, at rate 1/sqrt(N) or faster, provided the fluid limit has a global attractor.
results.proof: No new proof. The restricted problem is a multi-class restless bandit with a knapsack constraint: each session is an arm with state (class, idle age, held or not); holding is the active action and uses L tokens; a dropped arm stays passive until its return. It is indexable because the single-arm problem is an optimal stopping problem, in which the set of ages where holding is optimal shrinks as the price rises (checked numerically in the toy). The relaxed problem and its bound are results 6 and 7. The theorems then apply after two steps that are not done here: idle age is continuous and the gap laws are not exponential, so the arm must be approximated by finitely many phases; and the sizes L_i differ, so the constraint is a knapsack, which is covered when the largest L_i over C_H tends to 0. The global-attractor condition has to be assumed or checked for the fluid model.
results.draft_claim_checked: Result 10: 'Ranking by the index is asymptotically optimal for the relaxed problem as N grows (index-policy theory for restless bandits); cited, not re-proved.' Three corrections. (1) Wording: the index policy is asymptotically optimal for the hard-constrained problem; the relaxed problem supplies the bound it approaches. (2) Scope: the theory covers one resource, two actions per arm and arms that evolve independently. The design has three resources and several actions per session (hold, read, write, recompute), sessions coupled through the GPU queue and the device line (W, V, c and mu depend on everyone's actions, and in the closed loop the return times do too), and shared prefix heads. For that problem nothing is proved. The nearest results are for LP-based or fluid policies that are re-solved over time in weakly coupled problems with independent arms (Brown and Zhang 2022; Gast, Gaujal and Yan 2023), not for a static ranking by separate indices. (3) Conditions: the global-attractor condition is not a formality here, because campaign 32's loop is a second attracting state of the real system (result 9), so it holds at best with the born-clean and delay rules. N is 128 with about 40 to 60 prefixes in the host room (one prefix is 1.5 to 7 % of it), where a 1/sqrt(N) term is 10 to 15 %. The runs are two-hour transients, so the finite-horizon statement of Brown and Smith is the relevant one.

improvements: A provable optimum for the saturated regime: the floor. For every policy in the saturated closed loop, mean TTFT >= (N - B) g0 - Z + own prefill, reached when nothing is recomputed and no slot is left empty (result 8c). It is tight, it holds exactly where the Lagrangian bound fails, and the gap of a running system is observable: (N - B) x (recomputed tokens x gamma + empty slot-seconds x a/(B tau)) per request, about 1.6 s for campaign 34. Sketch: Little's law on the queue and on the running set, plus throughput falling with recompute and with empty slots.

One currency instead of two weights. Count lost GPU-seconds l = recompute seconds + loss from empty slots; then summed TTFT = base + (N - B) x l, exactly linear at saturation, not only to first order. c becomes a derived quantity: P(the slot stays empty) for the batch, (price of an idle GPU-second) x P(the GPU idles) for a single server. Fetch's lateness term and Retain's recompute term are then comparable by construction. Sketch: results 2(d) and 3(L4, L5).

A system-level due date for reads. Under pass-over a read is needed for the mean only when the GPU would run out of ready turns: T_starve = D + (ready turns behind) / (admission rate). Cost of landing at l: a fairness term on (l - D)+ for the turn itself and a mean term E[(l - T_starve)+]. Sketch: lemma L1 of result 3 while the ready backlog lasts, L2 after it. This makes c a quantity computed from the queue the engine already has, and explains why the hold never binds at saturation.

Estimators that match the proofs. mu = users in session - running turns once the pool has been full for one cycle time, otherwise 1 + Q/(1 - load) capped at that value. c = slot-seconds left empty while a turn waits on its read, over the stall-seconds (within 0.1 of the true value in simulation; section 6's estimator is too, for the batch). kappa = (late cost rates waiting + arrival rate x late cost rate x residual)/(1 - device load). lambda = time-average of the lowest index still held.

Device rule as one index plus a feasibility test: earliest due date while that schedule meets every due date, otherwise serve by w_j / max(p_j, d_j - t) (weighted modified due date; it reduces to Smith's ratio when all are late). Writes that free room for a read inherit d' = min(d_w, T_j - p_j). On random instances this costs 1.24 times the optimum in the mixed regime against 2.28 for the rule as drafted; the precedence part replaces the 50 K / 25 K thresholds and is optimal for the maximum lateness (Lawler 1973).

Preempt: use the skip variant of the greedy (factor 2 guaranteed; 5 % above the optimum on engine-sized instances against 39 % for the plain greedy), or the exact dynamic programme over pages (about 2e4 steps per event), and rank all classes in one list by surplus per token at the current price.

Tighter bound with time-varying prices. Replace the constants lambda and kappa by one multiplier per period (the dual of the constraint at each period, as in Brown and Smith). The bound stays valid for any non-negative path fixed in advance, the best path solves a convex problem, and the device term stops being empty. For the device alone, the conservation law of a work-conserving server gives a closed-form floor for linear costs (the c-mu value).

Stability as a design rule: no rationing action may create work for the rationed resource. In the model, if the write inflow does not increase with the dirty set (born clean, or delay), the clean state is the only fixed point and attracts every start; otherwise there are two stable states between a_max and a_loop. Two usable numbers: the clean reserve must keep dirty tokens below d_u(w) = d0 + (d1 - d0) p*(w)/p_max, and write priority alone removes the loop when the uncontended write rate exceeds a_loop (14.9 K tokens/s here; the write thread alone does 17 to 21 K).

State the regimes in users in session. With FA3 constants the pool fills at N_sat = B + Z/g0 = about 68 users (campaign 34's first sustained queue came at 76). Below about 50 users c = 1 and mu is 1 to a few; above about 72, c = 0 and mu = N - B. A light-load evaluation setting on this box should stay below 50 users in session; the M/M/1//N table in exp_mu.out gives mu across the knee.

Add a second criterion for who waits. At saturation the mean is blind to read timing, so Fetch and the device order have no optimum under the sum alone. With the longest reader stall as the second criterion, earliest due date is lexicographically optimal (result 4g), and the paper can report readers' TTFT as the quantity that rule minimises.

Make result 10 a theorem for the restricted problem: discretise idle age into phases, check the global attractor of the index policy's fluid equation numerically, and cite Verloop for several classes with a knapsack constraint; or use Brown and Smith's finite-horizon bound, which needs neither indexability nor the attractor and gives an explicit sqrt(N) gap for the two-hour transient.
